text: A veterans' hospital ward, not long after the war, filled with men in their twenties who will not walk again. Most of The Men stays inside that building, and the confinement is the point: whatever Ken has to work out, he works out among witnesses. He has refused to see the woman he was going to marry. That refusal drives the picture — less grief than arithmetic, a man deciding a fiancée is something he can no longer afford. Norm, Leo and Angel are not there to be inspiring; they know the rules of the ward and enforce them, roughly. Dr. Brock, who runs the place, talks like someone who has made this speech many times. Eighty-five minutes, and the tone stays low. The original screenplay took an Academy Award, and its virtue is how little it flatters anyone in the room.

In 1980 someone thought to point a camera at the Los Angeles punk scene before it had a history. Spheeris filmed Black Flag, the Germs, X, Fear, the Circle Jerks, Alice Bag Band and Catholic Discipline in the middle of their working lives, which produces a different film from the one an anniversary would make: the bands are not being commemorated, they are just playing this week. The camera stays close to the stage, and at these venues close to the stage means close to the floor, where the difference between performer and audience is mostly who is holding the microphone. What lasts is the ordinary detail — the rooms, the volume, the scale of a music made for a few hundred people at a time. It is in the National Film Registry.

The premise sounds like a joke and then declines to behave like one: Sherlock Holmes, deep in cocaine, tricked by Watson onto a train to Vienna and into the care of Sigmund Freud. Two methods are shut in one room, one that reads mud on a boot and one that reads a dream, and each is made to take the other seriously. There is also a case to run — a woman named Lola Deveraux has been taken — so the film keeps swapping a consulting room for a pursuit, and the seams show in a way a smoother version would not. The Vienna it builds is upholstered to the inch; the costumes won an Academy Award. Watson is the one to watch: a doctor who has lied to his friend for medical reasons and must now stand by while a stranger asks the questions.

Nine minutes, one abandoned mill, and weather coming across the fields. The catalogue files this 1937 cartoon under animation, family and music — and thriller, which is not a filing error. There is no story to speak of: owls, mice and nesting birds have taken over a building no longer good for anything else, and then the wind rises. What the film is after is atmosphere — dusk through broken slats, machinery waking when nobody has asked it to, the difference between a place at rest and a place under load. When the wheel starts turning, it is not a return to work; it is the building being operated by the storm. The peril belongs entirely to small animals and rotten timber, and it suffices: the short holds its shape without a single joke. It won the Academy Award for the year's animated short.

A priest is shot on a street corner in a Connecticut town, and every witness names the same stranger. Boomerang! then does the odd thing: it hands the film to the district attorney, Henry Harvey, whose job is to convict and whose problem is that the case has stopped convincing him. Kazan is less interested in who fired than in what a frightened town does to the men who work for it — the newspapers, the politics, the neighbours who saw a nervous out-of-towner and filled in the rest. Eighty-eight minutes, and the pressure sits in offices and hearing rooms rather than alleys. John Waldron barely gets to speak for himself; the argument goes on above his head, conducted by people whose futures depend on the answer. The screenplay was honoured at the Academy Awards.

The British Navy in 1797, and discipline aboard one warship is in the hands of a master-at-arms who enjoys the work. Ustinov directed, and he stays on the deck and in the space below it, where men live inside a system of law that offers no appeal and no way off. Billy is the newcomer, plainly good and incapable of suspecting anyone, and that innocence behaves on this ship the way a lit match behaves in a hold. Nothing is settled between two people here; everything passes upward through rank, through the captain, through what the regulations will permit. The talk is thick and formal, nearer to a stage than to sea adventure, and at just under two hours the film trusts that. One of the performances took an Academy Award for supporting actor.

Four Eugene O'Neill one-act plays were welded together to make a single crossing. The Glencairn is a merchant ship carrying cargo over the Atlantic in wartime, and the men aboard have a job, a war they are not fighting, and long hours with nothing to do but drink, argue and describe the rooms and farms they mean to reach. Ford leaves the episodic seams visible, so the picture moves the way a watch schedule moves — a night, a port, a night — rather than toward one climax. The photography is what the film is really about: black-and-white built from deck lamps and fog, faces lit from below, a freighter made to feel like a room with weather in it. It won an Academy Award for cinematography, and the war stays a rumour, with the ocean as the nearer problem.

Footage shot for the evening news turns out to be evidence, and the man who shot it is the last to know. John Cassellis is very good at his job, which means arriving quickly at other people's worst hours — violence, poor neighbourhoods, the racial temperature of the country — and cutting it to broadcast length. Learning that his network has been handing his reels to the FBI clarifies nothing; it only makes visible a transaction that was always part of the work. His toughness is a professional asset before it is a character trait, and the film keeps testing which it is. Made in 1969 about 1969, it has no distance to stand back into, and Wexler seems to want none. Nobody in it stays outside the apparatus, least of all whoever holds the camera. It sits in the National Film Registry.

A doctor tells a thirty-seven-year-old prizefighter that he can never fight again, and the picture is what the man does with the hours after that. Louis Rivera, called Mountain, has a face that records every year of the work and a vocabulary assembled entirely inside a gym. The trouble is practical before it is anything else: no trade, no schooling anyone will credit, a body that counts as an asset in exactly one building in the city. Nelson keeps the scale small — locker rooms, bars, the corridors where employment gets discussed — and lets the disproportion do the work, a large man briefly famous in a small way, negotiating with people who talk faster than he does. Ninety-five minutes, mostly interiors. The Directors Guild gave Nelson its award for the year.

Otis Redding, the Who, Jefferson Airplane, Simon & Garfunkel, the Mamas and the Papas: three days in California in 1967, cut down to eighty minutes. Pennebaker makes no attempt at the full programme — many of the musicians who played never reach the screen — and the editing treats a set the way a portraitist treats a face, taking one expression and leaving. The compression is the argument: this is what was worth keeping. Between numbers a concert film has to decide where to point, and the choices here run toward attention rather than spectacle, an audience in daylight working out how to behave. The Jimi Hendrix Experience is given a passage the film handles as an event in its own right. It is held in the National Film Registry.

Two of the three Carmodys want a house; the third wants the next road. That is the entire disagreement, and it takes a hundred and thirty-three minutes, because a family living out of a wagon in the Australian outback cannot settle an argument and then leave it behind — it travels with them, through shearing sheds, race meetings and other people's pubs. Zinnemann films the work as work: droving is a job, sheep are heavy, the weather decides the week. Paddy is not a wanderer with a philosophy, only a man who cannot picture himself standing still; Ida keeps her wanting quiet, which is harder to sit through than argument would be. Their teenage son is old enough to see that his parents' marriage is being decided by geography, and old enough to take a side.

The plantation is in Cochinchina, the nearest city is Saigon, and nobody ends up there by accident. Dennis runs the place; Vantine turned up because the Saigon police wanted a word with her; then the new surveyor arrives from home with a wife whose manners the compound has no use for. Red Dust is eighty-three minutes of proximity — one veranda, one heat, a handful of people obliged to be civil at meals — and the comedy and the cruelty come out of the same fact, that there is nowhere to be private. Vantine is the reason to stay: a woman already thrown out of one place, treating this one as somewhere to wait, and quicker than anybody else in the room. Fleming shoots it fast and close. The film is in the National Film Registry.

A Union private meets his own fear in his first engagement, and it is not a thought; it is his legs. Huston runs the whole film in sixty-nine minutes, which for a war picture is a decision rather than a shortfall: the war is only as wide as one soldier's line of sight, and that line is full of smoke, rumour and waiting. Henry Fleming's shame after he runs is entirely private, and the army around him is indifferent to it; regiments win and lose without noticing him. The fighting comes in bursts that end before anyone has understood them. At this length there is no room for the shape of a war, only the shape of a boy, and the compression keeps the tone flat and reportorial where a longer film would swell. It was named to the National Board of Review's ten best of 1951.

A mother walks across postwar Germany looking for her son, who is somewhere in the same wrecked country learning English from an American soldier. The Search was made in 1948, three years into the aftermath, a Swiss production shot in English, and its subject is less the war than the paperwork the war left behind: displaced children, offices, lists, the slow business of matching a name to a face. Zinnemann's attention goes to what the boy has already worked out about adults, which is that they arrive, sort people, and take them elsewhere. The GI's kindness has to operate against that education, and it cannot be argued; it has to be demonstrated, daily. A rescue story in which the machinery of rescue is part of the difficulty. The direction was recognised at the Academy Awards.
